```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "z282")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run scripts/09_z282_harmonisation.R first. ",
      "See the section 'Reproducing this'."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}

kArmOrder <- c("local", "central", "automated", "automated shared")

Arm <- function(frame) {
  frame$analysis <- factor(frame$analysis, levels = kArmOrder)
  frame[order(frame$analysis), ]
}

design <- ReadOutput("design.csv")
verdicts <- ReadOutput("claim_verdicts.csv")
```

## Why this dataset

- The three earlier reports each ended on the same admission. They could not
  measure how much of the spread in a flow result comes from the analyst,
  because that needs the same files gated by many people and each of them had
  one file or one operator.
- FlowRepository FR-FCM-Z282 is that design. Thirteen operators at five centres
  stained and acquired the same six samples on seven instruments, and they sent
  both the raw files and their own analysis to the coordinating centre [1].
- One reference operator then re-analysed all 234 files in Kaluza.
- The deposit therefore carries two complete answers for every file. The
  operator's own answer is the local analysis and the reference operator's
  answer is the central analysis.
- This report adds a third answer and a fourth. Both come from one automated
  rule that never sees either of the other two.
- The question the paper asks is whether centralising the analysis reduces
  variability. The question this report adds is which part of centralising does
  the work.

```{r}
#| label: design

kable(design, caption = "The deposit, counted from the file names and from the attached spreadsheet.")
```

- The design is balanced. Each of the thirteen operators contributes 18 files,
  which is two materials, three vials and three rounds.
- The frozen PBMC replicates were stained on three separate days, so they are an
  interassay measure. The whole blood replicates were stained on one day, so they
  are an intra-assay measure. That difference runs through every number below.

```{r}
#| label: operators

kable(
  ReadOutput("operators.csv"),
  caption = "Every operator, the centre they work in, the instrument they used and its model.",
  col.names = c("Operator", "Centre", "Instrument", "Instrument model")
)
```

## Part 1: what one pipeline has to survive

- The earlier reports named a channel once in a template CSV and reused it for
  every file. That is not possible here.
- Three makers name the same detector three ways. Becton Dickinson writes
  `PerCP-Cy5-5-A`, one operator configured the same analyser by laser and filter
  and it writes `Blue 670 LP-A`, and Beckman Coulter writes `FL4-A`.
- The sixth colour is not the same reagent in the two materials. It is the
  LIVE/DEAD Near-IR viability dye in the frozen PBMC panel and it is anti-CD45 in
  the whole blood panel, and both sit in the same detector.
- Some operators left the marker field empty, so those files carry a detector
  name and nothing else.
- The channel is therefore resolved per file, in two passes. The first pass reads
  the marker name the operator typed. The second pass falls back on the
  fluorochrome, through `gating/z282_panel.csv`.

```{r}
#| label: resolution

kable(
  ReadOutput("channel_resolution_summary.csv"),
  caption = "How each marker was matched to a channel across the deposit.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Resolved by", "Channels")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: pipeline-states

kable(
  ReadOutput("pipeline_states.csv"),
  caption = "Every state the pipeline had to detect before it could gate."
)
```

- The compensation state is not uniform either. Most Becton Dickinson exports
  carry a matrix with `APPLY COMPENSATION` set to `TRUE`, which means the values
  are already compensated. The Kaluza exports carry `$SPILLOVER` and no such
  keyword, so the matrix still has to be applied. Eighteen files carry no matrix
  at all.
- The scales differ as well. The measurement range is 262,144 on the Becton
  Dickinson instruments, 1,048,576 on the Gallios, and 1,024 on the eighteen
  files that one operator exported already scaled.
- A shared cut point across the deposit is therefore impossible. A value on one
  instrument's scale means nothing on another's, which is why every cut in this
  report is fitted inside one file or inside one operator.

```{r}
#| label: cut-rules

kable(
  ReadOutput("cut_rule_summary.csv"),
  caption = "Which rule produced each cut. The mixture only runs when the density carries no usable minimum.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Rule", "Cuts")
)
```

- The density minimum is the rule of first resort and it produced most cuts.
- A two component mixture is the fallback, and it exists because CCR7 and CD45RA
  are continuous. The paper says so in its own discussion, and the OMIP-039 and
  Yu 2021 reports met the same marker behaving the same way.

```{r}
#| label: failures

failures <- ReadOutput("gating_failures.csv")
kable(
  as.data.frame(table(reason = failures$reason)),
  caption = "Why a file could not be gated. The count is out of 234.",
  col.names = c("Reason", "Files")
)
```

- A file that cannot be gated is reported and dropped, not filled in.
- That is the lesson of the OMIP-043 report. A template that ran to completion
  and returned a number for a gate that had kept everything was worse than one
  that stopped.

### Two files of this deposit are one acquisition

```{r}
#| label: repeats

repeats <- ReadOutput("repeated_acquisitions.csv")
kable(
  repeats,
  caption = "Files that share an acquisition date, a start time and a GUID with another file.",
  col.names = c("File", "Operator", "Material", "Vial", "Round", "Date", "Time",
                "Events")
)
```

- These files carry different names and different checksums, and their FCS
  headers name the same acquisition.
- The design counts them as separate replicates. A repeatability measure computed
  over them understates the spread, because two of the three replicates are one
  measurement exported twice.
- The number is small and it is worth recording rather than smoothing over.

## Part 2: the paper's claims, from the deposit alone

- The twenty claims live in `gating/z282_paper_claims.csv`, each with the
  sentence it came from, so a reader can check the claim against the paper before
  the check of the number against the data.
- Every claim in this part is answered from the local arm and the central arm.
  The automated arms take no part in it.

```{r}
#| label: interoperator-counts

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("interoperator_counts.csv")),
  caption = "How many of the fifteen parameters meet each acceptability threshold. The paper sets CV below 0.20, bias below 0.20 and ICC above 0.75.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Parameters", "CV acceptable",
                "Bias acceptable", "ICC acceptable"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: interoperator-cv-figure
#| fig-cap: "Interoperator coefficient of variation, per parameter. The dashed line is the paper's acceptability threshold of 0.20."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("interoperator_cv.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: interoperator-icc-figure
#| fig-cap: "Agreement between operators, as the intraclass correlation of a two way random effects model. The dashed line is 0.75."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("interoperator_icc.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: intraoperator-counts

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("intraoperator_counts.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Repeatability within one operator. Each arm holds 195 measurements, which is 13 operators by 15 parameters.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Measurements", "Above 0.20", "Median CV",
                "Maximum CV"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: z-counts

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("z_counts.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Operator performance as a Z-score against the reference distribution. A score is unsatisfactory at 3 and questionable between 2 and 3.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Measurements", "Unsatisfactory",
                "Questionable", "Median absolute Z"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: z-figure
#| fig-cap: "Every operator and every parameter. Red is an overestimate against the reference value and blue is an underestimate."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("z_score_heatmap.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: verdicts

kable(
  verdicts[, c("claim_id", "short_name", "expected", "observed", "verdict")],
  caption = "Every claim the paper makes from the flow data, tested against the deposit.",
  col.names = c("Claim", "What the paper says", "Expected", "Measured",
                "Verdict")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: verdict-counts

kable(
  as.data.frame(table(verdicts$verdict)),
  caption = "How the twenty claims came out.",
  col.names = c("Verdict", "Claims")
)
```

- Several claims reproduce to the digit. The intraoperator maximum CV in frozen
  PBMC comes out at 1.32 local against 0.75 central, and the median at 0.13
  against 0.14, which is the paper's sentence exactly.
- The Z-score counts also land exactly. No score is unsatisfactory in the central
  analysis, one is in local frozen PBMC and 49 are in local whole blood.
- Those two hits matter more than the rest. They are computed from the paper's
  own definitions applied to the paper's own numbers, so an exact match says the
  definitions were read correctly before anything else was measured.
- The counts that miss by one or two come from the acceptability tables. The
  paper does not state whether a parameter exactly at a threshold counts as
  acceptable, and a difference of one parameter in fifteen follows from that
  choice alone.

### Where the deposit disagrees with the paper

- Claim 4 is the largest miss. The paper reports bias acceptable for 7 of 15
  parameters in locally analysed whole blood and this analysis finds 10.
- Claim 18 is the other one. The paper puts 63.9 percent of the naive and memory
  variance in the first two principal components and this analysis finds a higher
  figure.

```{r}
#| label: pca

kable(
  ReadOutput("pca_summary.csv"),
  digits = 1,
  caption = "Principal components on the centrally analysed whole blood values.",
  col.names = c("Group", "Variables", "Observations",
                "Variance in the first two components, percent")
)
```

- The paper centres and scales its data within each donor and each sample type
  before it runs the decomposition. This analysis scales across the whole set.
  The difference in the reported variance follows from that, and it is a
  difference in method rather than in the data.

## Part 3: two automated arms

- The automated arm applies one rule to all 234 files. It reads no operator's
  result and no reference value.
- The rule fits every cut on the file it gates, which is what an openCyto
  template does.
- The automated shared arm applies the same rule with one change. It takes the
  median of an operator's own fitted cuts, per marker and per material, and gates
  every file of that operator at that one value.
- The second arm exists because of what the first one showed, and because the Yu
  2021 report had already met the problem. That report fitted its cuts once on
  the pooled cohort, on the argument that a cut which moves with the sample
  changes a frequency for a reason that is not biology.

```{r}
#| label: shared-cuts

shared <- ReadOutput("shared_cuts.csv")
kable(
  head(shared[order(shared$operator, shared$material, shared$marker), ], 12),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The first twelve shared cut points. Each one is the median of that operator's own per file cuts, on that operator's own logicle scale.",
  col.names = c("Operator", "Material", "Marker", "Cut")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: distribution-figure
#| fig-cap: "The fifteen frequencies by arm. Every box holds the operator and donor means of one arm."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("distribution_by_arm.png"))
```

- The automated arms land close to the two human arms on the abundant
  populations and they drift on the small subsets. That is the pattern every
  earlier report in this repository found.

```{r}
#| label: intraoperator-figure
#| fig-cap: "Repeatability within an operator, by arm. The dashed line is the acceptability threshold of 0.20."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("intraoperator_cv.png"))
```

## Part 4: what the four arms say

```{r}
#| label: dispersion

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("dispersion_by_arm.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The median coefficient of variation across operators, pooled over the fifteen parameters and the three donors.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Median CV"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

- Read the intraoperator table and the interoperator table against each other.
  They answer two different questions and the two automated arms separate them.
- One cut per operator, in place of one cut per file, cuts the within operator
  spread by about a third in frozen PBMC and by a fifth in whole blood.
- The same change does not improve agreement between operators at all. The count
  of parameters with an acceptable CV and the count with an acceptable ICC both
  stay where they were.
- That is the finding this deposit makes possible. Holding a boundary steady
  across the files of one operator fixes repeatability. It does nothing for
  agreement, because each operator still holds a different boundary.
- The central analysis fixes both, and it fixes them for one reason. One person
  applied one judgement to every file of every operator.

```{r}
#| label: icc-after

kable(
  ReadOutput("icc_after_exclusion.csv"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Agreement in centrally analysed whole blood, before and after the operators outside a Z of 1.5 are removed.",
  col.names = c("Parameter", "ICC, all operators", "ICC, selected operators")
)
```

- The paper runs this same exclusion and reports that two parameters stay below
  0.75, and it names them as CD3-CM and CD4-CM. This analysis names the same two.

```{r}
#| label: size

kable(
  Arm(ReadOutput("cv_by_population_size.csv")),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "The median interoperator CV of the three parent populations against the twelve naive and memory subsets.",
  col.names = c("Arm", "Material", "Parent median CV", "Subset median CV"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

- Precision follows population size in every arm, including both automated ones.
- The three parent gates sit on markers with two clear modes. The twelve subsets
  sit on CD45RA and CCR7, which have no valley to find, and that single
  difference explains the whole gap.

```{r}
#| label: phenotype

kable(
  ReadOutput("phenotype_by_material.csv"),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The centrally analysed medians of each material.",
  col.names = c("Material", "CD4 percent of CD3", "CD8 percent of CD3",
                "CD4 over CD8", "CD8 terminally differentiated, percent")
)
```

- The paper flags the frozen PBMC preparation as carrying a CD4 over CD8 ratio
  below the expected value and a high proportion of terminally differentiated
  CD8 cells. The deposit says the same thing.
- The whole blood samples from the same study carry a normal ratio, so the
  anomaly belongs to the frozen preparation and not to the panel.

## Discussion

### What this shows

- A published harmonisation result reproduces from the deposited spreadsheet. Of
  the twenty claims encoded from the paper, most come out as stated, and the two
  claims that fix the definitions of every indicator come out to the digit.
- The gap that three earlier reports in this repository named is now measured.
  Thirteen analysts working on their own files disagree by far more than one
  analyst working on all of them, and the difference is largest in whole blood,
  where the material is easiest and the analysis is therefore the only thing
  left to vary.
- The two automated arms separate repeatability from agreement, which the paper's
  design cannot do on its own. A stable boundary fixes the first. Only a shared
  judgement fixes the second.

### Where the automated arms are weak, and why

- Both automated arms sit well below the two human arms on every indicator. That
  is the honest result and it is worth stating plainly rather than tuning away.
- Part of the gap is real. A rule that refits a boundary on every file follows
  the day to day drift in staining, and a person does not.
- Part of the gap is built into the comparison. The Z-score reference is the mean
  and the spread of the centrally analysed values, so any arm that differs
  systematically from the reference operator scores badly by construction, no
  matter how self consistent it is.
- The frozen PBMC arm carries the worst numbers and it also carries the hardest
  problem. Those replicates were stained on three separate days, so a per file
  cut has three days of drift to follow.

### What this does not show

- It does not show that the paper is right. It shows that the numbers in the
  paper follow from the spreadsheet the authors deposited.
- It does not separate the operator from the instrument. Two centres ran several
  operators on one analyser and one operator appears on more than one, so the
  design cannot attribute a difference to the person rather than to the machine.
- It does not measure the staining. Every operator stained their own tubes, so a
  difference between two operators holds the preparation, the acquisition and the
  analysis together. Only the local against central contrast isolates the
  analysis, because there the same file is read twice.
- The automated arms failed on some files and those files are dropped. A dropped
  file is not a missing measurement at random, because the files that fail are
  the ones whose densities do not resolve, which are also the ones a person finds
  hardest.

### What is left to do

- The 234 files come from 7 instruments and the design is unbalanced across them,
  so a variance components model with the operator, the instrument and the centre
  as separate random effects would say more than the indicators do. It is not run
  here.
- The reference operator is named as Op_M in the paper and the deposit is
  de-identified with a randomised operator code. The two are treated as the same
  letter in this report. That assumption is stated here because nothing in the
  deposit confirms it.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, 5.8 GB of the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/FR-FCM-Z282

# Derive the committed metadata from the deposit. It runs once, on the host.
uv run --project python python scripts/z282_derive_metadata.py

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The analysis
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  Rscript scripts/09_z282_harmonisation.R

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/z282_harmonisation.qmd
```

- The operator results are derived from the spreadsheet the authors attached to
  the deposit. They are committed as `gating/z282_operator_results.csv`, so the
  claim tests run without the 5.8 GB download.
- The 234 sample files are needed only for the two automated arms.

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
